title: Red carpet fashion
wikitext:
{{Short description|Outfits worn at major celebrity events}}
[[File:Beyoncé Knowles - Back - Los Angeles January 15, 2007.jpg|thumb|upright|American singer [[Beyoncé]] on the red carpet at the [[64th Golden Globe Awards]] on January 15, 2007]]

'''Red carpet fashion''' consists of outfits worn on the [[red carpet]] at high-profile gala celebrity events such as award ceremonies and film [[premiere]]s. The clothes worn to award events such as the [[Academy Awards|Oscars]] and the [[Golden Globe Awards|Golden Globes]] consistently receive intense worldwide media scrutiny, making their red carpets an international product placement area of great importance to fashion designers.<ref name=lenander/> Despite the publicity given to award ceremonies, other red-carpet events such as the ''[[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]]''-hosted [[Met Gala]] also have a significant impact on the fashion world.<ref name=FL>{{cite web|url=http://nymag.com/daily/fashion/2011/05/first_look_inside_the_met_for.html|title=First Look: Inside the Met for Tonight's Costume Institute Gala|access-date=2011-05-04|date=2011-05-02|work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]}}</ref>

==Red-carpet style==
===History===
[[File:Don Ameche and Cher.jpg|upright|thumb|right|alt=Cher in a revealing black Bob Mackie ensemble with a towering feathered headdress stands next to Don Ameche, who holds an Oscar statuette, at the 1986 Academy Awards.|[[Cher]] and [[Don Ameche]] on the red carpet at the [[58th Academy Awards]], 1986; Cher is wearing a [[Bob Mackie]] design]]

Until the end of the [[Classical Hollywood cinema|Golden Age of Hollywood]] in the 1960s and the emergence of [[New Hollywood]], the film industry operated under a studio system, where major studios like [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM]], [[Warner Bros.]], and [[Paramount Pictures|Paramount]] controlled nearly every aspect of movie production, including the public images of their stars. As part of this system, studios employed costume designers who were responsible for creating the wardrobes that actors wore on screen, as well as the outfits they donned for public appearances, including red carpet events.

Prior to the 1990s, celebrities often chose their own red-carpet dresses, with the Oscars being remembered for some extraordinary and eccentric outfit choices, including torn denim, sequinned jumpsuits and Indian headdresses.<ref name="lenander" /> ''Billboard''{{'}}s Brooke Mazurek wrote that as the red carpet emerged as a "cultural fixture" in the 1980s, American entertainer [[Cher]] "became one of its leaders".<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|title=How Cher Transformed Fashion And Became One Of The Most Influential Style Icons In Red Carpet History|first=Brooke|last=Mazurek|url= https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/lifestyle/7800945/how-cher-transformed-fashion-and-became-one-of-the-most-influential|date=May 19, 2017|access-date=September 8, 2020|url-status=live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170519173955/https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/lifestyle/7800945/how-cher-transformed-fashion-and-became-one-of-the-most-influential|archive-date=May 19, 2017}}</ref> At the [[58th Academy Awards]] in 1986, after being left off the Oscar nomination list for her lead role in ''[[Mask (1985 film)|Mask]]'', Cher wore a dramatic, tarantula-like Bob Mackie outfit that ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]''{{'s}} Esther Zuckerman later dubbed Cher's "Oscar revenge dress".<ref name=Zuckerman-VF>{{cite magazine |last=Zuckerman |first=Esther |url=https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2022/02/awards-insider-the-making-of-chers-oscar-revenge-dress |title=The Making of Cher's Oscar Revenge Dress |magazine=[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]] |date=February 3, 2022 |accessdate=February 20, 2022 |archive-date=February 4, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220204081714/https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2022/02/awards-insider-the-making-of-chers-oscar-revenge-dress |url-status=live}}</ref> Presenting the [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor|Best Supporting Actor]] nominees, Cher quipped, "As you can see, I did receive my Academy booklet on how to dress like a serious actress".<ref name=Lack-CNN>{{cite web |first=Hannah |last=Lack |url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/article/cher-remember-when/index.html |title=Remember when Cher wore a towering feather headdress at the 1986 Oscars? |publisher=[[CNN]] |date=May 20, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220211233536/https://edition.cnn.com/style/article/cher-remember-when/index.html |archive-date=February 11, 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

For ceremonies such as the Golden Globes, it was rare to see a star dressing up formally until the late 1990s, with many nominees turning up casually dressed.<ref name="merle">{{cite news|last=Ginsberg|first=Merle|title=The Psychology of the Golden Globes Dress|url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/psychology-golden-globes-dress-71546|access-date=20 June 2012|newspaper=The Hollywood Reporter|date=19 January 2011}}</ref> When [[Halle Berry]] came to the [[57th Golden Globe Awards|2000 ceremony]] in a glamorous white [[Valentino SpA|Valentino]] dress, it was described as a game-changer which set the standard for Golden Globe red carpet style, and according to [[Phillip Bloch]], her stylist at the time, "began the time when a dress could actually make a career."<ref name="merle" /> The increasing dependence on [[fashion stylists]] was something that had emerged since the 1990s, leading to criticism that red carpet fashion, particularly at the Oscars, now appears "bland and homogeneous", following a model of "discreetly elegant [[gown]]s, softly swept-up hairdos and lots of diamond jewellery".<ref name="lenander" /> The stylist's role is to try to ensure that the client only receives positive publicity for her appearance and is not featured on 'worst-dressed' lists.<ref name="lenander" /><ref name="perla">{{cite news|last=La Ferla|first=Ruth|title=The Power Stylists of Hollywood|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/01/15/fashion/hollywoods-power-stylists.html?_r=1|access-date=21 April 2012|newspaper=The New York Times|date=January 20, 2012}}</ref>

In 2004, ''[[The New York Times]]'', asking "Does the glamour of the Golden Globes steal the scene from Oscar?", observed that the wider range of potential nominees of the "younger, hipper" Globes, from television as well as film, offered designers more opportunity to have their work featured on the red carpet.<ref name=michault>{{cite news|last=Michault|first=Jessica|title=Does glamour of the Globes steal the scene from Oscar?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/02/28/news/28iht-roscars_ed3_.html|access-date=17 June 2012|newspaper=The New York Times|date=28 February 2004}}</ref> Unlike the Oscars, nominees for the Golden Globes and other events are under less pressure to choose an expensive, one-of-a-kind [[haute couture]] gown, which is also easier for the designers who can offer samples from their latest ready-to-wear lines.<ref name=michault/> One of the most widely publicised and talked-about red-carpet gowns was a ready-to-wear [[green Versace dress of Jennifer Lopez|green Versace gown]] worn by [[Jennifer Lopez]] to the [[42nd Grammy Awards]] ceremony on February 23, 2000.<ref name="PhillipsReay2002">{{cite book|editor1-last=Phillips|editor-first=Kim M.|editor2-last=Reay|editor2-first=Barry|title=Sexualities in history: a reader|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cz3bPMw_7h4C&pg=PA407|last=Barrera|first=Magdalena|chapter=Hottentot 2000: ''Jennifer Lopez and Her Butt''|access-date=16 May 2011|year=2002|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9780415929356|page=407}}</ref>

==Publicity==
[[File:Gabriel Garko and Laura Torrisi - nicogenin - 66ème Festival de Venise (Mostra) - The Road (3).jpg|thumb|upright|Italian actors [[Gabriel Garko]] (in [[black tie]]) and [[Laura Torrisi]] on the [[red-carpet]] at [[Venice Film Festival]], 2009]]

Having a dress featured on the red carpet, particularly one that attracts media attention, is very important to a designer, with [[Carmen Marc Valvo]] saying in 2000:

:"The dollar return of having some celebrity shot in your dress is worth a fortune, more than a five-page spread in ''Vogue'' or ''Harper's Bazaar'' that only appears once. That same image can be blasted repeatedly in newspapers and magazines across the country and around the world. That is worth hundreds of thousands of dollars."<ref name=parnes>{{cite news|last=Parnes|first=Francine|title=Dressing the Ladies|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=UmRWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NvIDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6516,476889&dq=golden-globes+2000+fashions&hl=en|access-date=17 June 2012|newspaper=The Spokesman Review|date=22 March 2000}}</ref>

A year after [[Kate Winslet]] wore one of his dresses to the 2002 Oscars, designer [[Ben de Lisi]] said:

:"I can't possibly quantify how much publicity I got from that or how much money I made. And now, every time anyone writes about her they use the picture of her in the dress and so it just goes on and on."<ref name=lisi>{{cite web|title=The Kate Debate: Ben de Lisi credits Kate Winslet for his booming business|url=http://www.vogue.co.uk/news/2003/06/13/the-kate-debate|publisher=British Vogue |access-date=18 June 2012|date=13 June 2003 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150222123312/http://www.vogue.co.uk/news/2003/06/13/the-kate-debate |archive-date= Feb 22, 2015 }}</ref>

This strategy is not without risk, as a designer may invest hard work and time into creating a unique dress (which could cost up to $100,000) for a celebrity, only to have their investment wasted when the star decides at the last moment to wear someone else's dress.<ref name="lenander">{{cite news |last=Lenander |first=Joanna |date=25 February 2005 |title=Why Oscar's Women All Look the Same |url=http://www.nysun.com/arts/why-oscars-women-all-look-the-same/9747/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120718022239/http://www.nysun.com/arts/why-oscars-women-all-look-the-same/9747 |archive-date=18 July 2012 |access-date=18 June 2012 |newspaper=The New York Sun |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref><ref name=parnes/> Particularly high-profile celebrities are often loaned dresses by several different designers for the ceremony, meaning that the designer often does not know until the night whether his or her dress was chosen to receive the much-desired exposure.<ref name=lenander/><ref name=parnes/> In addition, they run the risk of never getting the dress back, rejected or not.<ref name=parnes/> The choice for a designer may also be whether to dress one actress for the Oscars, or design an entire [[ready-to-wear]] collection.<ref name=michault/>

===Media===
Fashion commentary often forms a key part of the reportage of red-carpet events, both in dedicated shows such as ''[[Live from the Red Carpet]]'' and news reports such as those from [[BBC News]].<ref>{{cite web|title= In Depth: Oscars 2002|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/in_depth/entertainment/2002/oscars_2002/default.stm|publisher=BBC News |access-date=20 June 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title= Oscars 2011|date=8 February 2012 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-12252017|publisher=BBC News |access-date=20 June 2012}}</ref> Looks seen on the red carpet are also often featured in television shows on fashion, such as ''[[Fashion Police (TV series)|Fashion Police]]''. Until they retired in 2011, [[Joan Rivers]] and her daughter [[Melissa Rivers|Melissa]] presented televised reviews of red-carpet fashions from various ceremonies including the Academy Awards, the Golden Globes, and the [[Emmy Awards]].<ref name=hollywood-reporter>{{cite news|last=Guthrie|first=Marisa|title=Joan Rivers Says Her Red Carpet Reporting Days Are Over|url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/joan-rivers-red-carpet-reporting-69545|access-date=19 June 2012|newspaper=Hollywood Reporter|date=7 January 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Ram|first=Archana|title=Joan Rivers on her return to 'Fashion Police': 'The truth is very, very seldom said on television.'|url=http://popwatch.ew.com/2010/08/27/joan-rivers-on-her-return-to-fashion-police-the-truth-is-very-very-seldom-said-on-television/|publisher=Entertainment Weekly|access-date=22 June 2012}}</ref> In August 2007 Joan Rivers was replaced by [[Lisa Rinna]] as the host of [[History of Pop (American TV channel)|TV Guide Network]]'s red carpet coverage.<ref name=hollywood-reporter/>

==Cancelled events==
When the [[65th Golden Globe Awards]] ceremony was cancelled and replaced with a press conference as a result of a [[2007–2008 Writers Guild of America strike|writer's strike]] which also threatened the Oscars — this was also seen as a threat to the fashion industry.<ref name="Cieply">{{cite news|author1=Cieply, Michael |author2=Carr, David |name-list-style=amp |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/01/08/arts/television/08cnd-globes.html |title=No Golden Globes Show, Just a News Conference |access-date=January 8, 2008 |date=January 8, 2008 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Jolson|first=Jeffrey|title=NBC Cancels Globe Telecast, But will Stars Party On?|url=http://www.hollywoodtoday.net/2008/01/07/nbc-cancels-globe-telecast-but-will-stars-party-on/|access-date=17 June 2012|newspaper=Hollywood Today|date=7 January 2008|archive-date=16 June 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100616163002/http://www.hollywoodtoday.net/2008/01/07/nbc-cancels-globe-telecast-but-will-stars-party-on/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=strike>{{cite news|last=Jones|first=LaMont|title=Writers' strike is cutting fashion industry's red-carpet exposure|url=https://www.post-gazette.com/businessnews/2008/01/14/Writers-strike-is-cutting-fashion-industry-s-red-carpet-exposure/stories/200801140267|access-date=18 June 2012|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post Gazette|orig-date=14 January 2008 |date=16 March 2012 |version=republished}}</ref> Not only were established designers under threat, but the opportunity for up-and-coming designers to achieve widespread recognition through red-carpet exposure of their designs was severely limited.<ref name=strike/> In 2008, a number of events, including the threat of an actor's strike that would have led to cancellation of the [[81st Academy Awards|2009 Oscar ceremony]], and an upcoming star-studded [[First inauguration of Barack Obama|presidential inauguration]] had a visible effect on [[66th Golden Globe Awards|that year's Golden Globes ceremony]].<ref name=mich09>{{cite news|last=Michault|first=Jessica|title=Glamorous gowns win at the Golden Globes|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/01/13/style/13iht-rglobe.html|access-date=17 June 2012|newspaper=The New York Times|date=13 January 2009}}</ref> Many stars dressed for the Globes in unique couture gowns that they might otherwise have reserved for the Oscars.<ref name=mich09/>
